column1: # The eval's questions. Committed before any scoring code exists, deliberately:
# pre-registration only counts if the timestamps show it, and a question set
# committed alongside its results is indistinguishable from one written after
# seeing them.
# What is MIT's here, and what is invented
# MIT's, and therefore the part worth anything:
#   - the 20 documents, pinned by sha256 in `corpus.tsv`
#   - what each lecture is about, in `lecture_topics.tsv`, which is MIT's own
#     link text transcribed rather than interpreted
#   - the lecture ORDER, which is what "first occurrence" is measured against
# Invented for this eval, and therefore the part that limits what the number
# means:
#   - `query`. This is the largest degree of freedom in the whole measurement
#     and the place a score gets inflated without anyone intending to.
#   - `expected_first` and `relevant`, derived from MIT's titles by the rule
#     below. The rule is mechanical; choosing it was not.
# The honest comparison to keep in mind: the filename measurement was worth
# something because MIT wrote the filenames and the parser never saw them
# while it was being designed. Here MIT wrote the topics but a person wrote
# the questions, so this file is the eval's weakest link and is documented
# accordingly.
# The literal/paraphrase split, which is why this file has 16 rows and not 15
# ROADMAP asks for 15 questions. This is 16, as 8 matched pairs, and the
# deviation is deliberate: ROADMAP wrote 15 before this design existed, and a
# clean 8+8 split is worth more than matching the number.
# Every topic appears twice, once per phrasing:
#   literal     - built from MIT's own title words.
#   paraphrase  - the same concept with the title vocabulary removed.
# The reason is specific rather than theoretical. Page-1 headers in this corpus
# repeat MIT's lecture title verbatim, so a query phrased from that title can be
# answered by string overlap and reported as semantic retrieval. A literal
# question and a keyword baseline are looking for the same characters.
# So the two kinds are reported as separate rows and are NEVER pooled into one
# headline. Pooling averages a near-lexical match with a real one and hides
# both. Matched pairs rather than two independent sets: same topic, same
# expected answer, one variable changed, so the difference between the rows is
# the phrasing and not the difficulty of the topic.
# Writing the paraphrases is the most invented thing in this eval. They are
# committed here, before the scoring code, so they cannot be quietly reworded
# after a bad run.
# How `expected_first` and `relevant` were derived
# `relevant`  - every lecture whose MIT title covers the topic.
# `expected_first` - the lowest ordinal in `relevant`.
# Two consequences worth stating rather than discovering later:
#   - Ground truth is over TITLES, not contents. Sorting is arguably taught
#     before lecture 3 and recursion appears long before any lecture names it,
#     but MIT titles lecture 3 `Sorting`, so a hit on lecture 2 scores
#     first-wrong even where a person would call it defensible. That is a floor
#     on the achievable score and it is not retrieval's fault.
#   - `relevant` drives recall@k; `expected_first` drives the four-way tally.
#     Two relations out of one ground-truth file, both mechanical.
# Topics were chosen for having an UNARGUABLE relevant set. `Complexity`
# (lecture 19) was considered and left out for exactly that reason: every
# lecture in an algorithms course discusses complexity, so its relevant set
# would have been a judgment call, and an arguable ground truth undermines the
# thing the eval is for. The eight below are covered by MIT's titles and by
# nothing else.
# id<TAB>pair<TAB>kind<TAB>expected_first<TAB>relevant<TAB>query

column6: Where did I first learn about sorting?
How do I rearrange a list so that every item comes before the ones larger than it?
Where did I first learn about hashing?
How can I look up a key in constant time instead of scanning the whole collection?
Where did I first learn about binary trees?
What structure stores items in nodes that each point to a left and a right child?
Where did I first learn about binary heaps?
How do I repeatedly take the smallest item out of a changing collection quickly?
Where did I first learn about breadth-first search?
How do I explore a graph outward from a starting vertex, one level at a time?
Where did I first learn about depth-first search?
How do I walk a graph by following one route as far as it goes before backtracking?
Where did I first learn Dijkstra's algorithm?
Which method finds the cheapest route from one vertex when no edge has a negative weight?
Where did I first learn about dynamic programming?
How do I avoid recomputing the same subproblem by saving its answer the first time?
